entry.title: Do you really master LRU?
entry.content:
Every cache is a bet that you’ll want the same thing twice. Since caches are finite, every cache also needs an answer to an awkward question: when it’s full and something new arrives, what gets thrown out?

LRU is the most common answer. It’s also the answer that almost no production system implements literally. That gap is the interesting part.

1. What is LRU?

LRU stands for Least Recently Used. When the cache is full, evict whatever hasn’t been touched for the longest time.

The policy rests on one assumption: temporal locality. If something was accessed recently, it’ll probably be accessed again soon. This holds remarkably well for a lot of real workloads — web sessions, database pages, file blocks, CPU memory access.

It’s worth seeing where LRU sits among the alternatives:

PolicyEvictsTrade-off
FIFOOldest insertedTrivially cheap. Ignores usage entirely.
LRUOldest accessedGood default. Costs bookkeeping on every read.
LFULeast frequently accessedBetter for stable hot sets. Slow to forget old favourites.
RandomAnythingNearly free, surprisingly hard to beat by much.
Belady’s OPTThe item used furthest in the futureOptimal, and impossible — it requires clairvoyance. Used as a benchmark.

LRU wins as a default because it’s the cheapest policy that actually pays attention to what your program is doing.

2. Put it simply

Imagine your desk has room for exactly five sheets of paper.

You work through them all day. Each time you need a sheet, you pull it out, read it, and put it back on top of the pile. Sheets you use constantly keep floating to the top. Sheets you haven’t touched since morning sink toward the bottom.

Now a sixth sheet arrives and there’s no room. Which one do you get rid of? The one at the bottom — the one you haven’t touched the longest.

That’s LRU. The whole policy.

The subtlety is in how you maintain the pile. If you just dumped all five sheets in a heap and wrote the time on each one, finding the oldest would mean checking all five every single time. Fine for five sheets. Terrible for five million.

The trick that makes LRU practical is that you keep the pile sorted as you go, incrementally. Every access does one tiny bit of reordering work, so eviction is instant: just grab the bottom.

Which leads to the thing that makes LRU expensive in ways people don’t expect: every read is also a write. Reading from an LRU cache mutates it, because reading changes the order. Hold that thought — it’s why section 4 exists.

3. Implementations

The naive version

Store a timestamp with each entry. To evict, scan everything and drop the oldest.

Reads are O(1), evictions are O(n). For a small cache this is genuinely fine, and its simplicity has real value. For anything large it falls over.

The classic: hash map + doubly linked list

This is the canonical O(1) solution, and the one interviewers are fishing for.

Two structures working together:

  • A doubly linked list holds entries in access order. Most recent at the head, least recent at the tail.
  • A hash map maps each key directly to its node in that list.

The hash map gives you O(1) lookup. The linked list gives you O(1) reordering. Neither works alone:

  • A list alone means scanning to find a key — O(n).
  • A hash map alone has no notion of order.

The list must be doubly linked. To unlink a node in O(1) you need its predecessor, and only a backward pointer gives you that for free.

Both get and put are O(1). Memory cost is the payload plus two pointers per entry — 16 bytes on a 64-bit machine, which sounds trivial until you’re caching a hundred million small keys.

The sentinel head and tail nodes are worth noting. Without them, every unlink and insert needs null checks for “is this the only node,” “is this the first node,” and so on. With them, the list is never actually empty and the code has no branches.

The three-line version

Most languages ship this already. Java’s LinkedHashMap has an access-order mode built in:

Python’s functools.lru_cache decorator does it for function memoisation, and collections.OrderedDict exposes move_to_end() if you want to build it yourself. Go has container/list, and the community standard is hashicorp/golang-lru. C++ pairs std::list with std::unordered_map.

Reach for these first. Write the manual version when you need to customise eviction, or when someone’s asking you to on a whiteboard.

Where the textbook version breaks: concurrency

Here’s the practical problem. Since every read mutates the linked list, every read needs a write lock. A cache is usually read-heavy — that’s the entire point of a cache — so you’ve built a structure whose hot path is a global mutex. It becomes the bottleneck immediately under concurrent load.

Real systems escape this three ways:

  1. Shard it. Split into N independent caches keyed by hash. Contention drops roughly N-fold. Eviction is now per-shard rather than global, so it’s no longer true LRU, but it’s close enough and it’s the simplest fix that works.
  2. Buffer the accesses. Record reads into per-thread ring buffers and replay them onto the list later, in batches. Reads become lock-free. This is what Caffeine does.
  3. Stop tracking exact order. Approximate it with a bit or a coarse timestamp per entry. This is what almost every large system actually does, which brings us to the next section.

4. How real systems bend LRU

Textbook LRU has three problems at scale: the memory overhead of the pointers, the lock contention above, and one more that’s easy to miss.

Scan resistance. Suppose your cache is holding a nicely warmed hot set, and then some batch job does a single full-table scan. Every page in that scan is “recently used,” so LRU dutifully evicts your entire hot set in favour of data that will never be read again. One nightly report can destroy a cache’s hit rate. Pure LRU has no defence against this at all, because it can’t distinguish “used once, just now” from “used constantly.”

Here’s how different systems respond.

Redis: sample, don’t sort

Redis doesn’t maintain a global LRU list. Doing so would cost two pointers per object — for a server holding hundreds of millions of small keys, that overhead is unacceptable.

Instead, each object header carries a 24-bit clock timestamp, updated on access. When memory is tight, Redis picks a few random keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5), compares their timestamps, and evicts the oldest of the sample.

That’s it. It’s LRU by opinion poll. With 5 samples the result is a decent approximation of true LRU; raising the value gets closer at higher CPU cost. Redis 3.0 improved the accuracy by keeping a pool of the best eviction candidates seen so far, carried across rounds, so good candidates aren’t forgotten between samples.

Redis 4.0 later added LFU mode (allkeys-lfu), using an 8-bit logarithmic counter with time-based decay. The motivation is precisely the scan problem: with LRU, a key touched once ranks equal to a key touched ten thousand times.

Linux kernel: two lists, then many

The page cache uses a two-list strategy: an active list and an inactive list.

New pages land on the inactive list. They only get promoted to active on a second reference. Eviction pressure falls on the inactive list first.

This is scan resistance, cheaply achieved. A sequential read touches each page once, so those pages cycle through the inactive list and get reclaimed without ever displacing the genuinely hot pages on the active list. Ordering within lists is approximated with a referenced bit (CLOCK-style) rather than tracked exactly.

Linux 6.1 merged MGLRU (Multi-Generational LRU), which generalises two lists into multiple generations. Pages age through generations, and eviction targets the oldest. It reduced reclaim overhead substantially and improved hit rates under memory pressure.

MySQL InnoDB: insert in the middle

InnoDB’s buffer pool splits its LRU list into a “young” sublist and an “old” sublist, with new pages inserted at the boundary — about 3/8 of the way from the tail, not at the head.

There’s a second guard: innodb_old_blocks_time (default 1000ms). A page must survive in the old sublist for at least that long and be accessed again before it’s promoted to young.

Both mechanisms exist for the same reason. A full table scan reads each page once, in quick succession. Under textbook LRU it would flush the buffer pool. Under midpoint insertion, those pages never make it out of the old sublist.

CPU caches: pseudo-LRU

True LRU in hardware needs enough state to order every line in a set — impractical beyond low associativity. Processors use tree-PLRU instead, a binary tree of direction bits needing only n−1 bits per set. It points at an old line rather than the oldest. In silicon, close enough at a fraction of the cost is the right trade.

Caffeine: admission control

The most interesting modern variant. W-TinyLFU asks a different question — not “what should I evict?” but “should I admit this at all?“

A compact Count-Min Sketch tracks approximate access frequencies across a much larger key space than the cache itself holds. When a new item arrives and something must be evicted, the candidate is compared against the eviction victim, and the new item is only admitted if it’s more frequent. A small LRU window in front handles items that are genuinely new rather than genuinely unpopular.

The result is that a scan can’t pollute the cache — scanned items simply never earn admission. Caffeine consistently beats LRU on real-world traces, often substantially.

Worth also knowing: ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) balances recency and frequency using “ghost” lists of recently evicted keys, adapting its split automatically. ZFS uses it. PostgreSQL famously backed away from it over patent concerns and uses a clock-sweep algorithm instead.

5. Wrapping up

LRU is the right default. It’s simple, it matches how programs actually behave, and the hash map plus doubly linked list gives you O(1) on everything.

But notice what happened every time we looked at a real system. Nobody implements the textbook version, and they all deviate in the same three directions:

  • Approximate the ordering. Redis samples, Linux uses reference bits, CPUs use a bit tree. Exact recency ordering is rarely worth what it costs.
  • Segment the cache. Linux’s active/inactive lists, InnoDB’s young/old sublists, Caffeine’s window. Segmentation is how you buy scan resistance.
  • Filter what gets in. W-TinyLFU’s admission policy is the sharpest version of this, and the biggest departure from LRU thinking.

Those three moves are the actual lesson. LRU is one point in a design space defined by memory overhead, lock contention, and how badly a sequential scan can hurt you. Knowing where your workload sits on those axes matters more than knowing the data structure.

And if you’re preparing for interviews: implement the linked list version until it’s automatic, then be ready to explain why the read path needs a write lock. That second question is where the conversation gets interesting.

References

  • Redis: Key eviction — sampling, the eviction pool, and LFU mode
  • Redis LRU implementation notes — antirez on why approximation was the right call
  • MySQL: Buffer Pool LRU algorithm — midpoint insertion parameters
  • Linux MGLRU documentation — the multi-generational design
  • Caffeine: Efficiency — W-TinyLFU benchmarks against LRU and ARC
  • TinyLFU: A Highly Efficient Cache Admission Policy — Einziger, Friedman & Manes
  • ARC: A Self-Tuning, Low Overhead Replacement Cache — Megiddo & Modha, FAST ‘03
  • LeetCode 146: LRU Cache — the standard exercise

entry.title: Phone Detox Experiment
entry.content:
Before the experiment 🧠

Actually, getting lost scrolling through my phone has been a common thing for many of us, especially in a modern world, where we are always connected with others through social media. High tech IT companies hire top talents to design delicated algorithms, striving to stick users to their product, and then make profits. Don't be guilty for that, it's not our fault. That being said, we still ought to view this matter objectively. Internet grant us access to abundant information, yet we should not get trapped by cognitive overload.So, I decided to try a phone detox experiment, help me discover a world that I could talk more with myself.

Experiment design

As usual, here’s the 7-day plan of “Phone Detox Experiment”. I made this plan with ChatGPT based on my own experience. Hope I will follow the plan strictly🤣.

Daily note 🤔

Day 1

Target: Awareness - How often I reach for devices?

The day has just begun, I’m hoping to get off to great start💪. We’ll wait and see

  • 8:30 – I woke up, and started my day. The first thing I did was to check my phone for new notifications from Gmail and Wechat. Then sitting on the toilet, I scrolled through Reddit threads about new AI workflow and car modification stuff…
  • 11:30 – Shortly after I wrote down the plan, I felt the urge to scroll TikTok to check if I’d gotten any likes👍🏽. Bloody hell…
  • 14:00 – Went to the toilet, scolling through RedNote for what’s new around me, like car exhaust clips, new harness usage, and stock market exploding news.
  • 17:00 – Working out, frequently checked my phone during set break, even there weren’t any new messages. It’s like a built-in background check, yep, this isn’t the thing I expected.
  • 19:00 – Listening to English podcast when cooking, thinking that I shouldn’t waste any piece of time…
  • 23:30 – Went to bed, and listened to some audio fiction books to help fell asleep, for 30min…

Wrap up: I felt like I was good enough to keep me away from the phone, but actually I was just get lost depending on information from my phone constantly. Maybe it’s because of information anxiety, which means my inner mind is to to as much information as I could get, otherwise I would fall behind. Hah, typical Chinese guy🐼.

Day 2

Target: Embrace of BOREDOM

Today, I wouldn’t use phone during waiting time and toilet time. In my opinion, if I could make it then I am a total “badass🏎️”

  • 8:00 – Got up, going directly to wash and brush teeth. Then cook breakfast without even thinking of the phone, although sometime I could hear a voice from my built-in “bad” system told me to check my phone for something INTERESTING (actuall 99.99% useless content).

  • 9:00 – Went to school, and started my day without taking phone with me. In fact, I felt kind of frustrated that I couldn’t get some “happniess” from time to time.

  • 9:30 – It feels just like quitting alcohol. Even though, I’ve never gone through it myself, my brain was constantly itching to open all unread messages.

  • 12:30 – Done 10min meditation, enduring the “tedious” moment, trying to feel the temperature of my breathe, as well as the noise of the silence. After that, I felt way easier to start working on my school tasks.

entry.title: Caffeine Detox Experiment
entry.content:
Before the experiment 🧠

When it comes to having coffee, I would think of my experience in TikTok. When it was during the COVID-19 pandemic, I felt so depressed that I tried various ways to help me felt better because of getting quarantined at home. I got a cup of hand brewed pour-over coffee one day, and it was so fabulous. That's how my coffee dependency kicked off. Coffee did bring lots of happy experience to me. That said, coffee has also brought me troubles. For instance, I usually force myself to be awake through iced latte after burning the mid-night oil. I feel I am "awake", but actuall my brain has already broken down. How do I know that? Cuz I was like a "zombie", easy to forget things, hard to retrieve even simple info from memory.I'd say drinking coffee in a correct way would greatly improve life quality. I decided to try a caffeine detox experiment though. Just want to know if it helps.

Experiment design

Owning 0 experience about this field, I do some research online. And here’s a plan, I made it clearer by ChatGPT visualization.

Here’s the 7-day plan of “Caffeine Detox Experiment”, I’d append my daily report below in next 7 days.

Daily note 🤔

Day 1

Target: Cut down – Reduce usual intake

Felt kind of happy and unhappy today. Feeling happy is because I’m making things different and trying something new to help me with my health. Feeling unhappy as I will lose some of my 🙃dopamine source.

Maybe this is the last cup of coffee I will drink this week. Tomorrow, I will try with tea or a little bit instant coffee.
By the way, simple coffee bean here is so simple in Auckland, at least in most of cafe. Maybe I didn’t get the correct way to be a coffee enthusiast here. I used to having special coffee beans in BeiJing, sometimes I have to admit that there are some benefits for “workforce advantage”🤣.

Day 2

Target: Limit to half

Got up early to go boat fishing, and drank a canned coffee to woke me up. Nothing chanllenging, nothing special. Just got seasick 🫠

Day 3

Target: No caffeine

Do sleep well last night, I got up at near 8am today.Still half-asleep, I made myself a cup of coffee. Then pour it down the sink… Anyway, I felt a little bit dizzy and headache, but it’s okay.

Day 4

Target: Experience the toughest day

Realllllllly tough, even I had a good sleep last night, but during the day I felt a little bit dizzy and headache. Moveover, I couldn’t focus on anything. After 2 hours of struggle, I finally went into the flow.

Meanwhile, I also found that it was vulnerable to get scrolling throught the screen when I couldn’t gather my mind. Just for reminder, keep phone away from me.🤛

Knocked out a few sets of back exercises, my head felt much better after that💪🏽

Day 5

Target: Energy improves

Easily went to sleep last night, get up early today. I go for a walk outside and love soaking up the sun☀️. Even no other coffee, I can also be engergized.

Day 6

Target: Reach a new balance

I kind of feel nice today, without thinking about coffee or something that gives me dopamine. It’s like I were a flat person, being easy to satisfy and come into a state of flow.
Free of distracting thoughts, the mind flows like a gentle, murmuring stream.

Day 7

Target: Natural energy coming back!

Beauuuuuuutiful day! Got up naturally even without alarm clock~ Full of energy all the day and have a car meetup with my friend.
Less “cache miss”, more “cache hit” when retrieving information from memory.

Conclusion🧑🏿‍💻

For me personally, I think the experiment works well. I felt much better after the experiment. I can also focus on my work more easily.That said, I won't give up drinking coffee or something with caffeine thoroughly, instead I would try to reduce the intake. After all, special coffee is fabulous.

entry.title: Reflection - System Design Process
entry.content:
For a long time I sat on the other side of the table. I interviewed a lot of candidates on system design, and the pattern was consistent: the ones who struggled had no frame to hang the problem on. They’d dive straight into databases or microservices and then get lost. The ones who did well slowed down and worked through the problem in an order that made sense.

I ended up on the interviewee side recently, and I wanted a process I could actually follow. The infographic is what I landed on.

Six phases, roughly 10 minutes each, totalling about an hour.

👔Step 1: business use cases (10 min)

Before any technical decision, understand the problem.

Who are the users? What are they actually trying to do? What does “working” look like?

This is the easiest step to skip and the hardest to recover from. If you get the use cases wrong, you’ll end up with something architecturally coherent that solves the wrong problem. Interviewers notice when candidates jump straight to components. The ones who do well ask questions first.

🦾Step 2: constraints (10 min)

Once you know what, figure out how much.

What’s the expected QPS? What latency does the use case actually need? How much data? What’s the availability target?

Don’t skip budget, timeline, or compliance. Real systems have real limits. Stating constraints explicitly gives you something to point back to when you make trade-offs later.

🏰Step 3: architecture (10 min)

Now draw the high-level picture.

What are the major components? Where are the boundaries? What technology are you choosing, and why? Walk through the data flow.

This doesn’t need to be a final production design. It needs to be a coherent skeleton that can hold up to questions. Show that you can decompose a complex system into parts someone else can follow.

⌨️Step 4: API design (10 min)

With the architecture sketched, define the contracts between components.

What are the key endpoints? What do requests and responses look like? How do you handle auth, errors, versioning?

Candidates often get vague here. Interviewers who’ve worked in production know that badly designed APIs cause pain for years. Be specific.

📊Step 5: database choice (10 min)

Pick the right storage layer, and explain why.

SQL or NoSQL depends on your data model, access patterns, and consistency requirements. Talk about sharding, indexing, caching, failure handling.

The point isn’t to always reach for the same tool. It’s to show you can reason about trade-offs: read-heavy vs write-heavy, strong vs eventual consistency. Rattling off database names without that reasoning doesn’t go far.

📀Step 6: data model (10 min)

Finally, get concrete about the data.

Define your entities and their relationships. Specify primary keys and indexes. Think about what happens to the schema at scale.

A well-thought-out data model often exposes assumptions from earlier steps that don’t hold up. That’s a good sign. Going back and revising shows you’re thinking through the problem, not filling out a template.

Wrapping up

Keep it simple, communicate clearly, iterate and refine.

That’s mostly it. The interview isn’t asking whether you know every database or can sketch the perfect architecture in 10 minutes. It’s asking whether you can navigate an open-ended problem without losing the thread.

The six steps are a scaffold, not a script. Practice it enough that it becomes automatic. Then the mental energy you’re not spending on process can go toward the parts of the problem that are actually hard.

entry.title: The Silent Performance Killer - False Sharing in C++
entry.content:
One day I ran into a weird performance issue when tunning the ring buffer module of a high performance C++ RPC framework.

I cooperated with another colleague, aiming to write a fast ring buffer, somehow he updated the key struct definition, we weren’t on the same page though.
Eventually the performance benchmark ended up performing poorly.

In hindsight, the degradation was not directly a bug in the code, but a feature of the hardware. In our benchmark, the throughput under 2 threads was better than that of 8 threads, which was really interesting.

That was caused by false sharing, one of the most counterintuitive performance bugs in concurrent C++.

TL;DR

  • False sharing occurs when multiple threads access and modify variables that reside on the same cache line, leading to a degradation in performance.
  • False sharing can be avoided by using padding or alignment to separate variables on different cache lines.

What’s False Sharing?

False sharing happens when threads modify variables that happen to live on the same cache line. The variables themselves are unrelated, but the cache line keeps bouncing between cores, invalidated over and over, and that’s what kills the performance.

Feynman Method


Imagine you and a colleague are sharing a single whiteboard, but you each only need one small corner of it.

You’re writing your notes in the top-left corner. Your colleague is writing theirs in the top-right corner. You never touch each other’s work. Completely independent.

But here’s the catch: the whiteboard can only be erased and rewritten one person at a time. Every time you want to write something, you have to claim the whole whiteboard, which means your colleague has to stop, wait for you to finish, then reclaim it before they can write again. And vice versa.

Neither of you is doing anything wrong. You’re not interfering with each other’s content at all. But you’re constantly blocking each other from using the board, because the rule operates on the whole whiteboard, not on individual corners.

That whiteboard is a cache line. Your corner is variable x. Your colleague’s corner is variable y. The “claim the whole board” rule is the MESI coherence protocol.

The fix is simple: get a second whiteboard. Put your notes on one, your colleague’s notes on the other. Now you never have to wait for each other. That’s what alignas does, it forces each variable onto its own cache line, its own whiteboard, so the two cores never have to fight over the same one.

Start with an Example

Consider the following code snippet:

Building and running this gives:

  • When false-sharing:
  • When fixed:

The performance result gap is significant, it costs 1776 ms to run the code snippet with false-sharing, while 409 ms to run it with fixed false-sharing issue.
And it will be even worse if we run it on more cores.

When reproducing the case by yourself, it should be noted that:

  1. We should compile with -O3, otherwise the compiler will optimize away the false-sharing issue. Sepecifically, it will simply remove the loop and add the final result. It was like “You nerd, why not add the variable all at once??”.

  2. We should use volatile to ensure that the compiler doesn’t optimize away the access to the variables in the example. Otherwise, the variable is cached in the CPU register, making it hard to observe the performance degradation. Since it optimizes away a ton of DRAM memory access.

Under the Hood

CPUs don’t read individual bytes from RAM. They read in fixed-size chunks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes on most modern x86 and ARM processors. When a core accesses any byte in memory, the entire 64-byte line containing it is pulled into L1 cache.

This is usually a win. But in multithreaded code, it creates a trap.

Suppose Thread A writes to x and Thread B writes to y. Different variables, different threads, no logical sharing. But if x and y sit within the same 64-byte cache line, the CPU doesn’t know that. Every time Thread A writes, it acquires exclusive ownership of the line, which invalidates Thread B’s copy. Thread B then reloads the line before it can write. Then A’s copy is invalidated. Back and forth, millions of times per second.

This is false sharing: threads that don’t share data logically, but are forced by hardware to behave as if they do.

The mechanism is the MESI cache coherence protocol. A write transitions a cache line to Modified on the writing core and broadcasts Invalid to all other cores holding a copy. Each invalidation costs dozens to hundreds of cycles and they never stop.

Solution

Method1: Padding

By adding padding to the struct, we can separate the variables onto different cache lines, which avoids false sharing. In C++, we can use keyword alignas to align the variables.

The padding happens during compilation phase by adding padding bit between the variables.

Method2: Thread local

Another way to avoid false sharing is to use thread-local storage by rethinking the design if possible.
By declaring the variables as thread-local, each thread gets its own copy of the variable, which avoids false sharing.
It’s like:

Caveats

  • Padding wastes memory. A padded char occupies 64 bytes instead of 1, and for a large array of padded structs, that 8x memory bloat can hurt cache efficiency at a higher level than the false sharing you were fixing.

  • 64 bytes is the common cache line size on x86/ARM today, but it isn’t universal. Prefer std::hardware_destructive_interference_size over hardcoding the number.

  • True sharing is a different problem. If two threads genuinely need to access the same variable, padding does nothing, that’s a synchronisation problem, not a layout problem.

  • To confirm false sharing is actually the cause, run perf stat -e cache-misses ./xxxx on Linux. A suspiciously high cache miss rate under the parallel workload is usually the tell.

  • False sharing happens at every cache level, but it hurts worst at L1. Each core’s L1 and L2 are private, so when two cores write to variables on the same cache line, the coherence protocol keeps invalidating those private copies. The reloading core usually finds a valid copy in the shared L3 (about 40 cycles) instead of going all the way to RAM, since the contested line stays hot in the hierarchy from the other core’s writes. The cost isn’t the fetch distance, it’s how often the invalidation happens: a 4-cycle L1 hit turns into a 40-cycle L3 reload on every single write. Across NUMA sockets with no shared L3, it gets worse still.

Key takeaway

entry.title: What's true understanding?
entry.content:
Recently I’ve taken a class in UoA called “Self-Leadership”, which has given me a great deal of food for thought. It was somewhat novel and unfamiliar to me, and I mistook it for a typical self-success course.
But the course content turned out to be surprisingly insightful. I’ve learned the most fundamental practice of self-leadership: reflection. There is no secret formula or magic behind it. It simply offers me a quiet chance to pause, slow down, and reflect on my inner self.

TL;DR

  • The illusion of understanding is a common trap in learning, where we feel like we understand something but lack genuine mastery.
  • Use Feynman’s Method to check if you understand the concept.

Observation

These days I spent plenty of time diving into CSAPP, a classic book in computer science. Over the past few years in my work, I always intended to read this book thoroughly, but never got around to it.

What I found interesting is that I acted differently. I somehow took on two distinct approaches once I began learning basic concepts such as Virtual Memory and Set Associative Caches.

To summarize, I understand Set Associative Caches better than Virtual Memory. Meanwhile, reading the chapter on Virtual Memory felt more enjoyable and rewarding. In contrast, studying the other topic is quite challenging and “full of dopamine”.

Inflection

Why?
It is an issue with the illusion of understanding. It is recognition, yet not genuine mastery.

When I closed the book, and looked back at the whole picture of Virtual Memory. I asked myself, but I got stuck over and over again. I couldn’t clarify the details of the concept, and I came up with some new questions. It ended up the knowledge is like a cyclone, it comes and goes, leaving a mess.

I think the reason is that I used to use Virtual Memory a lot in my work. Therefore, I just read the concepts happily without stop thinking more about it. There was a voice in mind said “Yeah, that’s it. The layout is just like that. The underlying mechanism is just like that.”. I was so satisfied that I had learnt so much again. (Maybe after several days, I could be “happy” once more). 😔

In terms of Set Associative Caches, it’s not a huge knowledge, so I break it down into smaller parts and draw diagrams to help me understand it better. I somehow map the diagrams in my mind, and start explaining it to myself. Every time I get stuck by something that I can’t make it clear, I just go back to the book and read it again. Eventually, I really master it! I can spot connections between it and my existing knowledge. 😁

Implication && Action

I may have tried these methods consciously or unconsciously before. But now I need to define them clearly and supervise myself to see if I can put them into practice 👊.

  1. Thinking about how to articulate the ideas without opening the book. Actually it’s Feynman’s Method. Personally, I can understand about 90% of new knowledge after using the Feynman Method.
  2. Drawing diagrams to help me understand the concepts better.
  3. Break down the knowledge into smaller parts, making it easier to take action.

Attachment

Here’s the Pros. and Cons. of using Feynman’s Method, just for you information.
